title: Regime-Aware AI Post-Processing of Monsoon Rainfall Forecasts
department: National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF)
description:
• Problem Statement Rainfall forecast errors over India vary with weather regimes such as active monsoon, break monsoon, monsoon lows/depressions, orographic rainfall, coastal rainfall and western disturbances. A single bias-correction method may not work equally well in all situations.The challenge is to build an AI/ML-based rainfall post-processing system that first identifies the prevailing weather regime and then applies suitable correction to the raw NWP rainfall forecast.The aim is to improve district/grid-level rainfall forecasts, especially for heavy and very heavy rainfall events.
• Expected Outcome Expected Outcome - Description:
Weather regime classifier - Classification of active, break, depression,coastal/orographic rainfall regimes Bias-corrected rainfall forecast - Improved rainfall forecast compared to raw NWP output Heavy rainfall probability - Probability of rainfall exceeding operational thresholds District-level rainfall product - User-friendly rainfall forecast table/map Verification report - Skill comparison using RMSE, ETS, CSI, POD, FAR and FSS
summary: Innovation (4/5): draws on ai, ml applied to a disaster management problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (4/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a working prototype is realistic in a 36-hour window. Impact (4/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Disaster Management. Tech Depth (2/5): centers on moderate engineering scope. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (2/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 19/30 -> Yellow verdict.

detail.title: Regime-Aware AI Post-Processing of Monsoon Rainfall Forecasts

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a system that first figures out which monsoon 'mode' India is currently in, active, break, depression, then applies the right correction to raw rainfall forecasts for that specific mode, instead of using one bias-correction method for every situation.
overview.why_it_matters: A single correction method doesn't work equally well across different monsoon regimes. Getting the regime-specific correction right directly improves rainfall forecast accuracy where it matters most, heavy rainfall events.
pain_points: Rainfall forecast errors vary systematically by weather regime (active monsoon, break, depression, orographic, coastal).
A single bias-correction method applied uniformly doesn't work well across all these different regimes.
No system currently identifies the regime first before applying targeted correction.
overview.background: Monsoon rainfall forecasting errors vary by regime, but current bias-correction approaches don't adapt to the specific prevailing weather regime, limiting forecast improvement especially for heavy rainfall events.
overview.whats_being_asked: An AI/ML rainfall post-processing system that first classifies the prevailing weather regime, then applies regime-appropriate bias correction to raw NWP rainfall forecasts.
expected_solution: Weather regime classifier (active, break, depression, coastal/orographic).
District-level rainfall product with formal skill verification (RMSE, ETS, CSI, POD, FAR, FSS).

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Moderate-High. Regime-aware post-processing (classify first, then correct) is a real, technically sound improvement over uniform bias correction, genuine meteorological ML sophistication.
analysis.invention_effort_note: Low-moderate as scored, achievable using established classification and bias-correction techniques applied thoughtfully to this two-stage regime-aware architecture.

competitive_landscape.note: Genuinely technical meteorological post-processing PS, appeals to a team with real forecast-verification interest, a narrower field.

innovation.note: Regime-aware, two-stage correction (classify then correct) is a genuinely sound technical improvement over uniform bias correction.

invention.note: Achievable using established classification and post-processing techniques, real effort in correctly implementing the two-stage architecture.

technical_feasibility.note: Public NWP rainfall forecast archives and observed rainfall data exist for training and the formally-named verification metrics.

impact_and_benefits.note: Directly improves heavy rainfall forecast accuracy, a genuinely high-value operational improvement given monsoon rainfall's importance.

architecture.note: A two-stage classifier-then-corrector pipeline, well-understood pattern, real value in correct regime definitions.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Strong pick, genuinely well-scoped with explicit, standard meteorological verification metrics named (RMSE, ETS, CSI, POD, FAR, FSS), giving a rigorous, credible way to demonstrate real improvement over raw NWP output.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: The PS explicitly names standard meteorological verification metrics, giving a rigorous, professionally-recognized way to demonstrate genuine forecast improvement, not a made-up success metric.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Building bias correction without genuine regime-classification (or with a poorly-defined regime classifier) would undermine the whole premise, the correction is only as good as the regime identification feeding it.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Invest real effort in correctly defining and validating your regime classifier first, the entire premise of this PS depends on genuinely distinguishing active/break/depression/coastal regimes, not an arbitrary or oversimplified classification.

idea_0_4: Source public NWP rainfall forecast archives and observed rainfall data (district-level, if available) for a monsoon season test period.
Research the actual meteorological definitions of the named regimes (active monsoon, break, depression, orographic, coastal) to build a genuinely meaningful classifier.
Split: one person on the regime classifier, one on the regime-specific bias-correction models.
prototype_4_22: Build your regime classifier using historical/current weather pattern data.
Build regime-specific bias-correction models, applying a different correction depending on the classified regime.
Start computing the named verification metrics (RMSE, ETS, CSI, POD, FAR, FSS) against your test period's actual observed rainfall.
integration_22_30: Connect classifier and regime-specific correction into one end-to-end pipeline.
Compute your full verification metric suite comparing your regime-aware corrected forecast against the raw NWP baseline.
Test specifically on heavy/very heavy rainfall events, since the PS emphasizes this as the priority use case.
polish_30_36: Build a clean district-level rainfall product visualization (table/map) as the PS requests.
Prepare your verification report with the named metrics comparing your approach against raw NWP, this is your core evidence.
Rehearse explaining your regime classifier's logic and why regime-aware correction genuinely improves over uniform correction.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Present your full verification report with the named professional meteorological metrics (RMSE, ETS, CSI, POD, FAR, FSS), showing genuine, quantified skill improvement over raw NWP output specifically for heavy rainfall events, that rigor is exactly what the PS is asking for and most teams won't do this thoroughly.

strengths: Explicit, standard verification metrics named give a rigorous, credible way to prove real improvement.
Genuinely sound technical approach (regime-aware two-stage correction) with real meteorological grounding.
weaknesses: Requires genuinely meaningful regime classification, not arbitrary categories, which needs real domain research.
Computing the full named verification metric suite correctly takes real statistical/meteorological care.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: Don't skip the verification-metrics role, computing RMSE/ETS/CSI/POD/FAR/FSS correctly is real statistical work that directly proves your value claim.
team_fit.approach: Research the real meteorological definitions of each named regime before building your classifier, arbitrary or oversimplified regime categories undermine everything downstream.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Standard classification model scaffolding and bias-correction techniques.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Correctly defining and distinguishing the named weather regimes based on real meteorological criteria, and correctly computing/interpreting the standard verification metrics, that's genuine domain and statistical expertise.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: A poorly-grounded regime classifier (arbitrary categories not reflecting real meteorological distinctions) would undermine the entire premise, since the correction quality depends entirely on genuine regime identification accuracy.

data_resource_availability.status: Public NWP rainfall forecast archives and observed rainfall data genuinely exist and are accessible for real training and rigorous verification.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: Not needed, real data access is achievable here.

judge_qna.question: How does your regime classifier actually distinguish active monsoon from break monsoon from depression conditions?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Walk through your specific classification features and criteria, grounded in real meteorological indicators (e.g. specific rainfall patterns, pressure systems), not an arbitrary or oversimplified rule.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's your classifier's accuracy against known, documented regime periods?

judge_qna.question: What's your actual skill improvement over raw NWP output, using the standard metrics?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Present your specific RMSE, ETS, CSI, POD, FAR, and FSS results comparing your regime-aware correction against the raw baseline, real numbers, not a general improvement claim.
judge_qna.follow_up: Does the improvement hold consistently across all regimes, or does it help more in some than others?
